title: Redwood Private VPC security architecture deep dive with Monarch Financial
summary: Deep dive on Redwood Private placement into Monarch's VPC/on-prem strategy. Covered SOC2/ISO evidence, SSO and SCIM provisioning, customer-managed KMS/HSM integration, audit log flows to Splunk, and network controls (ingress, egress, private endpoints, firewall rules, bastion). Agreed next steps: share architecture diagram, security pack, and schedule a bench test with egress policy examples.
next_steps: Redwood to share Private VPC architecture diagram and security pack by 2026-10-12
Customer to provide current network diagram and NAT/egress policy by 2026-10-15
Schedule bench test for egress-restricted calls (30-min) week of 2026-10-19

transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-10-07
Start: 15:00 UTC
Duration: ~62 minutes
Attendees: Olivia Chen (Redwood AE); Diego Reyes (Redwood SE); Mark Holloway (Monarch CISO); Priya Nair (Head of Infra); Sam Li (Network Eng)

AUTO-GENERATED SUMMARY (may be incomplete):
- Deep dive on Private / VPC private deployment topology, network isolation, ingress/egress controls, and compliance artifacts.
- Discussed customer-managed KMS and HSM, audit log forwarding to Splunk, SAML/SCIM provisioning, RBAC roles, and SOC2 requirements.

Transcript:
[00:00] Olivia: hey everyone thanks for joining, appreciate you making time. quick roll call?
[00:07] Mark: Mark here, hi.
[00:09] Priya: priya on infra.
[00:11] Sam: sam li, network.
[00:13] Diego: diego from redwood se.
[00:15] Olivia: great, so goal for today is a technical deep dive on our private vpc/on-prem options focused on security, compliance and the network controls. we'll surface any gaps and next steps.

[02:01] Diego: ok quick overview — redwood private runs a control plane we can host either in your account or our control plane with customer-managed network boundaries, but for monarch you mentioned you want everything inside your vpc, is that right?
[02:18] Mark: yes, our compliance team is clear — data must not egress to vendor-owned networks, and all keys managed by our KMS or HSM. so we need private-only endpoints, strict egress, audit logs into our splunk cluster, and SOC2 evidence.
[02:38] Olivia: understood. two typical patterns — 1) full private deployment where the control plane sits in your VPC and we run agents in your subnets, or 2) hybrid with private endpoints (privatelink) and customer-managed egress controls. both support SOC2/ISO.

[04:12] Priya: can you expand on the privatelink pattern? we prefer not to run extra compute if possible.
[04:20] Diego: sure — with privatelink we expose service endpoints that are reachable through interface endpoints in your VPC so traffic never traverses the public internet. requests go from your app -> VPC endpoint -> redwood service over AWS backbone. you can lock down security groups and NACLs around the endpoint. this also allows you to keep egress locked down because there is no need for NAT for that traffic.
[04:53] Sam: sounds good but what about egress to other redwood-managed services like telemetry or updates? we need to control where those go.
[05:02] Diego: good call. we support two options — allowlist egress to specific aws ranges / ip sets, or a customer-managed forwarder: you can route all redwood egress through a customer-hosted bastion or proxy in your subnet which then forwards to allowed endpoints. we also provide an on-prem connector for air-gapped sites where you don't want any outbound connectivity except a controlled channel.

[06:30] Mark: and encryption? keys must be customer-managed and rotated under our KMS/HSM. we can't have vendor keys.
[06:38] Olivia: absolutely — we support customer-managed KMS for data at rest. for even higher assurance we integrate with HSM-backed key stores; we can do envelope encryption so your keys encrypt per-customer master key. Diego can speak to the mechanics.
[06:55] Diego: yes envelope encryption pattern — model artifacts and persistent storage are encrypted with a data key; that data key is encrypted by your KMS CMK. Redwood never sees the plaintext master key. we also support KMS that supports external key manager (XKM) and HSM sign-off. some customers require an HSM for signing and FIPS-proof attestation which we can integrate with.

[08:30] Priya: ok audit logs — we need all request/response metadata (no PII) forwarded to our splunk with retention of seven years and immutable logs where possible. do you provide a syslog/s3 forwarder?
[08:47] Diego: we can ship audit logs to a customer S3 bucket or stream into your SIEM via syslog/splunk HTTP event collector. note that transcript/full-response payloads can contain sensitive data, so by default we redact those and only forward structured metadata unless you opt into additional fields. we keep an append-only write pattern and digital signatures in the log to aid tamper detection.
[09:30] Sam: also need proof of chain-of-custody — how do we prove logs weren't altered?
[09:36] Diego: we sign log batches server-side and you can verify signatures with a public key; if you want customer-side signing we can route logs through your collector that applies your signing.

[11:00] Mark: SOC2 and ISO evidence — what artifacts do you provide?
[11:07] Olivia: we have a security pack: SOC2 report, ISO cert, penetration test summary, architecture diagrams, third-party pen test remediation items. i'll share the pack after the call.
[11:18] Mark: please include your sysadmin access controls and RBAC matrix.
[11:23] Olivia: yes will include RBAC roles, SAML integration notes, and our support access process (break-glass + auditable approvals).

[12:10] Priya: SSO — we want SAML with SCIM provisioning. can you do delegated SSO and SCIM provisioning to map groups to roles?
[12:19] Diego: yes, we support IdP-initiated and SP-initiated SAML, and SCIM for provisioning. role mapping is configurable: you can map SAML attributes or SCIM groups into our RBAC (admin, infra, audit, viewer). we also support short-lived tokens and session timeouts aligned with your policy.
[12:45] Sam: auditing changes to RBAC configs is critical. does the UI and API produce an auditable changelog?
[12:52] Diego: yes — all admin actions are logged with actor, timestamp, and diff of the config change. those logs can be forwarded to your SIEM.

[14:30] Olivia: network flow specifics — how do you want us to show ingress/egress? we can provide sample security group rules, NACLs, privatelink configuration and terraform snippets.
[14:42] Priya: terraform snippets would be ideal; our infra is mostly IaC. also we need to validate no unintended open ingress from internet.
[14:51] Diego: we'll include example security group rules that only allow traffic from app subnets to the interface endpoint, and example NACL entries. for egress we show either NAT-based allowlists or proxy-based forwarding through a bastion with strict allow rules.

[16:20] Sam: what about mTLS between services? we have internal requirement to use mTLS for service-to-service.
[16:27] Diego: we support mTLS for service connections inside the VPC. Our sidecars can use client certs signed by your CA, or if you prefer, we can integrate with a service mesh. note: mTLS adds operational complexity for key rotation but it's supported.

[18:05] Priya: packet-level controls — do you require any open ports for health checks? our firewall team will block everything by default.
[18:13] Diego: typically for interface endpoints you don't need additional inbound ports; if you run agents in your subnets, we recommend health checks on high-numbered ephemeral ports that are internal-only. we can also expose health on a localhost-only endpoint and use the agent to push health to your monitoring.

[20:00] Mark: the big ask is demonstrable proof we can run without any egress to vendor networks except through customer-managed proxies. can we run a bench where we restrict egress to only a whitelisted IP and show model responses?
[20:12] Olivia: yes, we can set up a bench test. diego will draft the egress policy and a test plan.

[22:30] Diego: one caveat — some model downloads and container images may be large; if you want fully air-gapped we support an offline image transfer workflow where you pull artifacts via a secured channel and import them into your private registry. otherwise we can pre-cache images in your account with initial egress for the sync, then lock it down.
[23:02] Priya: ok we'll probably want the offline sync for initial onboarding.

[24:40] Sam: can you summarize the firewall / ingress / egress rule set we should expect?
[24:46] Diego: sure — 1) Ingress: only from internal app subnets to the interface endpoint or agent; no public ports. 2) Egress: either no egress (offline) or egress via a customer NAT/proxy with allowlisted destinations (we'll provide IP ranges). 3) Internal: mTLS between agents/services, security groups to enforce least privilege, NACLs for subnet-level defense. 4) Monitoring: flow logs to s3 + siem, VPC flow logs for forensic.

[27:10] Mark: retention & data residency — logs must stay in our s3 in us-east-1 and all compute in the same region.
[27:19] Diego: that's fine — we can pin region and avoid cross-region replication. we also support custom S3 endpoints for govcloud if needed.

[29:05] Priya: who holds support access keys? we need a break-glass process with time-limited access and full auditing.
[29:13] Olivia: yes break-glass via ticketed request, ephemeral role assumption with just-in-time access, and full session recording. We also have a policy that support engineers cannot access customer data without explicit approval and each session is logged.

[31:00] Sam: monitoring/alerting — how do you integrate with our pager/duty and our SIEM?
[31:06] Diego: we push alerts to your pagerduty via webhook and forward logs to your SIEM. we can also create per-route latency and error alerts that forward to your ops channel.

[33:10] Mark: any third-party dependencies we should be aware of that might affect compliance?
[33:17] Diego: we use oss components and some cloud provider managed services (e.g., S3, KMS). we'll provide a third-party dependency list and SBOM for the runtime.

[35:00] Priya: network testing — will you provide terraform to stand up the privatelink endpoints and security groups so we can code-review?
[35:08] Diego: yes terraform snippets and example policies. we'll include terraform for interface endpoints, security group, NACL, and an optional example of a forwarding proxy instance.

[37:40] Olivia: let's talk timeline — what does monarch want for a pilot?
[37:45] Mark: pilot should be in our staging vpc with no outbound internet except to our splunk collector and redwood privatelink endpoint. succeed metric: latency under 250ms p95 and no data leakage; security metric: all logs forwarded to splunk and keys under our KMS.

[38:10] Diego: sounds reasonable. we will produce a test plan that includes egress-restricted calls and key rotation.

[40:00] Sam: any constraints on internal network ranges? we use RFC1918 ranges and some overlapping subnets with vendor accounts — do you support VPC peering or sidecar deployments?
[40:10] Diego: we support both. for overlapping ranges we recommend interface endpoints (privatelink) to avoid peering CIDR conflicts. if peering is preferred we can do NAT and route table controls, but privatelink is simpler for isolation.

[42:30] Priya: how will you validate that responses don't contain sensitive PII in logs?
[42:36] Diego: we have a redaction pipeline that removes or hashes patterns recognised as PII by our pipeline. for additional assurance we can route full transcripts to a customer-managed collector where you run additional DLP checks before storing.

[44:00] Mark: operations — who runs patching of agents or runtime components in our VPC?
[44:07] Diego: if agents run in your account, you control patching cadence; we provide updates and a rolling upgrade plan. for managed instances we run updates but only after agreeing windows and patch notes; everything is auditable.

[46:30] Priya: compliance evidence for SOC2 — do you provide machine-readable attestations or just pdf reports?
[46:36] Olivia: primarily PDF reports for SOC2/ISO and machine-readable artifacts like audit log exports, SBOM, and config diffs. we'll include the SOC2 cover letter and scope delineation.

[48:00] Sam: firewall team will want exact egress ip ranges. will you provide them?
[48:05] Diego: yes, we'll provide a stable set of ip ranges for the privatelink egress endpoints and examples for the proxy flow. if you prefer CIDR ranges we can provide those, otherwise we provide an fqdn list that your egress proxy resolves.

[50:00] Mark: what about support for encrypted request-at-rest in transit — do you terminate TLS at our endpoint or at redwood?
[50:08] Diego: for privatelink traffic TLS is end-to-end; you can provide certs for mutual TLS. for agent-based deployments traffic never leaves your VPC in plaintext. we can also support customer-provided TLS termination at an internal ALB if that's your architecture.

[52:30] Priya: final question: do you support revocation of access if we terminate contract and ensure keys are not usable?
[52:37] Olivia: yes we have a decommission runbook. keys under your KMS remain with you; we remove access policies and rotate service-side keys. we also provide a secure deletion checklist and support for forensic export before shutdown.

[55:00] Diego: i'll summarize technical deliverables — 1) terraform snippets for privatelink & security groups, 2) sample egress policy and bench test plan, 3) audit log forwarder config and splunk HEC example, 4) KMS/HSM integration notes and envelope encryption pattern, 5) offline image transfer steps.

[56:05] Olivia: ok next steps again: i'll send the security pack; diego will share terraform + bench test; priya and sam will share vpc and egress requirements.

[58:30] Mark: thanks everyone this was helpful.
[58:34] Priya: thanks, talk soon.
[58:36] Sam: thanks.
[58:38] Olivia: thanks — end call.

NOTES/IMPERFECTIONS: transcription shows occasional speaker mislabels and minor word-swaps (e.g., kv cache -> kv cash). some timestamps are approximate.
